title: The Printer and the Paper Money: Boston, Philadelphia, Craven Street, Passy
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Milk Street, the fifteenth child
stops.date_confidence: attested. Born 6 January 1705 by the Julian calendar then in use in the British colonies; 17 January 1706 is the Gregorian equivalent after the 1752 reform, and is the date used throughout this file.
stops.campa: Josiah Franklin boils soap and dips candles on Milk Street, and this son is the fifteenth of seventeen children. The house stands across the way from the meeting house. The boy goes to Boston Latin School at eight and is taken out again before ten, because his father cannot carry the cost of a son destined for the church. That is the whole of his schooling. Everything he knows afterward he takes out of books he sets in type himself, and out of arguments with men in rooms he organizes for the purpose.
suggested_refs: The Milk Street birthplace site, marked by a bust on the Old South Building, Boston

stops.name: Old South Meeting House, baptized the same day
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the same-day baptism. The brick meeting house on this site dates from 1729; the 1706 baptism took place in the earlier cedar Third Church building on the same ground. Coordinate corrected to the Wikipedia value, about 140 m east of the figure this research first produced.
stops.campa: He is carried across the street and baptized on the day he is born. Josiah Franklin left Northamptonshire for the right to sit in a room like this one, gathered by its own members and answering to no bishop. The son will spend his life among Anglican prelates, French Catholic ministers, and Parisian deists, and will keep from this ground one habit only: he treats a congregation as a thing men assemble for themselves, which is also how he will treat a library, a fire company, a philosophical society, and eventually a country.
suggested_refs: Old South Meeting House baptismal records, Boston
sources: Old South Meeting House historical records
Isaacson, Benjamin Franklin: An American Life (2003)

stops.name: James Franklin's shop, the apprenticeship
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: At twelve he is indentured to his brother James, printer, for nine years. He learns the case, the composing stick, the press, the smell of lampblack and oil. He reads everything that passes through the shop and quarrels with his brother about most of it. The trade he takes here he carries to London, back to Philadelphia, and finally to a rented mansion at Passy, where at seventy-one he sets up a press and prints passports for a country that does not yet legally exist. He signs himself printer for the rest of his life, including on his own epitaph.
suggested_refs: The site of James Franklin's printing house, Queen Street, Boston

stops.name: The New-England Courant, Silence Dogood
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1722 for the Dogood letters and James Franklin's three-week imprisonment; month approximate. The whole episode reaches us only through Franklin's own Autobiography, written some fifty years later, so one lens of this research tagged it reconstruction on sole-witness grounds.
stops.campa: James founds Boston's third newspaper and Benjamin, sixteen, slides anonymous letters under the shop door signed Silence Dogood, a country widow with opinions about ministers, funerals, and hoop petticoats. The shop prints them without knowing that the author is setting their type. When James is jailed three weeks over what the paper carries, the apprentice runs the paper alone. The next year he breaks the indenture and runs, which in the law of the colony is the theft of himself. The only witness to any of it is the man remembering it half a century later.
suggested_refs: Surviving issues of The New-England Courant, 1721-1723, and the fourteen Silence Dogood letters

stops.name: Market Street wharf, the arrival with the rolls
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1723; the day is not recorded and defaults to 01.
stops.campa: He comes up the Delaware with almost no money, buys three great puffy rolls, and walks up Market Street with one under each arm eating the third, past the door where Deborah Read is standing. He records that she thought he made a most awkward ridiculous appearance. Pennsylvania makes its first paper money the same year he lands, and forty-four years later he writes that before it came the trade was carried on by barter, and that the paper gave new life to business. The runaway apprentice and the colony's currency arrive in the same town in the same season.
stops.quote: The difficulties for want of cash were accordingly very great, the chief part of the trade being carried on by the extremely inconvenient method of barter; when in 1723 paper-money was first made there; which gave new life to business, promoted greatly the settlement of new lands.
stops.quote_source: Benjamin Franklin, 'Remarks and Facts Relative to the American Paper-money' (1767), Complete Works vol. 3, Project Gutenberg e-text #48138
suggested_refs: The Market Street wharf landing site, Philadelphia

stops.name: Bartholomew Close, the London printing houses
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1724-1726 London stay; the coordinate is Palmer's house in Bartholomew Close, and the stop also carries Watts's house near Lincoln's Inn Fields (about 51.5158, -0.117), where he moved in 1726.
stops.campa: Governor Keith of Pennsylvania promises to set him up in a shop of his own and sends him to London to buy type, then sends no letters of credit after him. Franklin lands at eighteen with nothing and works as a compositor at Samuel Palmer's house in Bartholomew Close, then at the larger house of John Watts near Lincoln's Inn Fields, where the pressmen mark him for drinking water and carrying more type up the stairs than the men who drink beer. He is learning the streets of a city he will spend eighteen later years arguing with.
suggested_refs: The site of Palmer's printing house, Bartholomew Close, Smithfield
The site of Watts's printing house, Wild Court, near Lincoln's Inn Fields

stops.name: The Junto, the club of tradesmen
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1727; month and day default to 01. The meeting place is a reconstruction, not a documented address. The chronology and geography lenses of this research disagreed on whether the Junto itself is attested or reconstructed, the source in both cases being the Autobiography.
stops.campa: Back in Philadelphia he gathers a surveyor, a shoemaker, a joiner, a glazier, a clerk, and himself into a club that meets Friday evenings to put questions to each other about morals, politics, and natural philosophy. The rules forbid direct contradiction and positive assertion. Out of this room come the subscription library, the fire company, the hospital, the academy, and the American Philosophical Society. Not one of them holds a degree and the club owns no building; they meet in a tavern room, and later in a member's house.
stops.quote: 'For a word to the wise is enough,' as Poor Richard says... 'God helps them that help themselves,' as poor Richard says.
stops.quote_source: Benjamin Franklin, 'The Way to Wealth' (preface to Poor Richard Improved, 1758), Complete Works vol. 3, Project Gutenberg e-text #48138
suggested_refs: Franklin's list of twenty-four standing queries for the Junto, in the Autobiography

stops.name: Franklin and Meredith, the shop on Market Street
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1728; month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: He goes into partnership with Hugh Meredith, whose father puts up the money, and opens a printing house on Market Street. The work is job printing: pamphlets, blanks, handbills, whatever the colony needs set in type. He keeps his hours visible, wheeling his own paper through the streets on a barrow so that the town can watch him working, and stays away from the fishing parties and taverns where a creditor might see him idle. Within two years he will own the press outright and be printing the colony's money on it.
suggested_refs: The Franklin Court archaeological site, Market Street, Philadelphia

stops.name: Burlington, printing New Jersey's money
stops.date_confidence: attested by Franklin's own Autobiography and by Van Doren, for 1728-1729; month and day default to 01. One lens of this research downgraded this to tradition; verification restored it to attested.
stops.campa: The partnership takes a government contract and Franklin crosses the Delaware to Burlington to print New Jersey's paper currency, lodging there for months while the sheets come off the press. He is twenty-two and handling the physical manufacture of a colony's money: the plates, the counts, the signatures, the risk of a forged impression. He will later press real leaves into the plates, so that the veins of a leaf, which no engraver can copy by hand, sit on the face of the bill. The counterfeiter's problem is solved as a printer's problem.
suggested_refs: Surviving New Jersey and Pennsylvania colonial bills bearing Franklin's nature-printed leaf impressions
sources: Isaacson, Benjamin Franklin: An American Life

stops.name: Market Street, A Modest Enquiry
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1729; day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Pennsylvania is short of coin and the argument over printing more paper splits the town: the common people want it, the rich men holding debts do not. Franklin, twenty-three, prints an anonymous pamphlet: money is the measure of trade, and a province with too little of it pays high interest, loses its laborers to colonies that have more, and leaves its land unsettled. He is arguing for the paper, and he owns a press that can print it. He will spend the rest of his life defending colonial paper before English boards of trade.
stops.quote: About this time there was a cry among the people for more paper money, only fifteen thousand pounds being extant in the province, and that soon to be sunk.
stops.quote_source: Benjamin Franklin, The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Project Gutenberg e-text #148
suggested_refs: A Modest Enquiry into the Nature and Necessity of a Paper Currency, Philadelphia, 1729
sources: Franklin, A Modest Enquiry into the Nature and Necessity of a Paper Currency (1729)

stops.name: Market Street, the Gazette and the currency contract
stops.date_confidence: attested. Franklin and Meredith bought the Pennsylvania Gazette from Samuel Keimer on 2 October 1729; Franklin became sole owner in July 1730 on buying Meredith out. The day of the buyout defaults to 01. An earlier pass of this research wrongly made him sole owner in 1729.
stops.campa: In October 1729 he and Meredith buy The Pennsylvania Gazette from Samuel Keimer; the next July he buys Meredith out and holds paper and press alone. In the same season his friends in the Assembly reward the pamphlet by handing him the contract to print Pennsylvania's currency. He now prints the province's newspaper and the province's money, out of the same shop, off the same presses, at twenty-four. He sets the arrangement down in his memoir as one more advantage gained by being able to write.
stops.quote: My friends there, who conceiv'd I had been of some service, thought fit to reward me by employing me in printing the money; a very profitable jobb and a great help to me. This was another advantage gain'd by my being able to write.
stops.quote_source: Benjamin Franklin, The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Project Gutenberg e-text #148
suggested_refs: Bound runs of The Pennsylvania Gazette, 1729-1748
Pennsylvania colonial currency printed at Franklin's press

stops.name: Market Street, Deborah Read and the boy William
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1 September 1730 as the date of the common-law union. William Franklin's birth is dated by tradition to 22 February 1730, but the sources range from 1728 to 1731 and no acknowledgement event is dated anywhere reachable.
stops.campa: On the first of September he takes Deborah Read as his wife by common law. Her first husband has vanished and cannot be proved dead, so a licensed marriage would expose them both to a charge of bigamy. Into the same household comes William, his son by a mother no source names, born around this year, the date disputed in every account. Deborah raises him. Fifty-five years later, at Southampton, this boy will be a deposed royal governor living in London on a crown pension, and the two of them will meet as men who have chosen opposite sides.
suggested_refs: Philadelphia records of the Read family and the disappearance of John Rogers

stops.name: Library Company, the first subscription library
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1731; day defaults to 01. Franklin's initiation into Freemasonry at St John's Lodge is attested to the same year, but no reachable source fixes that lodge's meeting place, so it is carried in this stop rather than given a pin of its own.
stops.campa: The Junto pools its books, then goes further: fifty subscribers pay forty shillings down and ten shillings a year, and the money buys from London what no one member could buy alone. It is the first subscription library in the colonies. In the same year he is initiated into Freemasonry at St John's Lodge in Philadelphia, whose meeting place no surviving record fixes. The books are kept in a member's rooms and go out to subscribers one at a time, against a deposit of their value.
suggested_refs: The Library Company of Philadelphia's founding articles of 1731 and its first London book order
sources: Library Company of Philadelphia institutional history

stops.name: Market Street, Poor Richard begins
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1732 for the first almanac, issued for the year 1733; the December publication date circulates in the literature but was not confirmed against a primary source this session.
stops.campa: He invents a poor astrologer named Richard Saunders with a nagging wife and an urgent need for money, and publishes an almanac in his voice: weather, tides, eclipses, court days, and in the margins the proverbs. Most of them he takes out of older English collections and files each one down to a shorter line. It runs every year to 1758 and sells about ten thousand copies annually in a colony of a quarter million people. The printer who argued for more paper money spends twenty-five years teaching his customers thrift.
stops.quote: Drive thy business, let not that drive thee; and early to bed, and early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise, as poor Richard says.
stops.quote_source: Benjamin Franklin, 'The Way to Wealth' (preface to Poor Richard Improved, 1758), Complete Works vol. 3, Project Gutenberg e-text #48138
suggested_refs: The run of Poor Richard's Almanack, 1733-1758, and the 1758 preface later titled The Way to Wealth

stops.name: Philadelphia, Grand Master and Anderson's Constitutions
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1734; month and day default to 01. Coordinate is Franklin's Market Street press, where the reprint was set, not a lodge room.
stops.campa: Three years after his initiation the Pennsylvania brethren elect him Grand Master, and he sets in type a reprint of James Anderson's Constitutions of the Free-Masons, the first Masonic book printed in the Americas. Anderson's volume carries the craft legend of Hiram Abiff, the master builder murdered at Solomon's temple, out of the London Grand Lodge founded at the Goose and Gridiron in 1717 and onto a colonial press. George Washington will be initiated at Fredericksburg eighteen years after Franklin sets this type.
suggested_refs: Franklin's 1734 Philadelphia reprint of Anderson's Constitutions of the Free-Masons

stops.name: Philosophical Hall, the American Philosophical Society
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1743 for the founding proposal; month and day default to 01. The coordinate is Philosophical Hall, built in 1785, not the society's first meeting place.
stops.campa: He circulates a printed proposal for a standing society of virtuosi drawn from every colony, corresponding by post about botany, mechanics, medicine, and any improvement to the ordinary business of living. It is the Junto scaled to a continent, and it works only because the same man is building the post. Philadelphia is named as the center because it sits nearest the middle of the colonies and has the best communication with the rest. The society outlives the empire that never chartered it, and will one day hold his own papers.
suggested_refs: Franklin's 1743 broadside, A Proposal for Promoting Useful Knowledge Among the British Plantations in America

stops.name: Franklin Court, the press handed off
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1748; month and day default to 01. No source reached this session names the partner who took over the press.
stops.campa: At forty-two he is rich enough to stop. He turns the printing house over to a partner on a share of the profits and keeps the income coming in without setting a line of it. What he does with the time instead is electricity, stoves, and the colony's business. Half a life remains and none of it will be spent setting type for hire. Looking back at the paper money he argued for and then printed, he grants that the quantity has limits beyond which it can do harm, which is a thing the pamphlet of 1729 did not say.
stops.quote: The utility of this currency became by time and experience so evident as never afterwards to be much disputed; so that it grew soon to fifty-five thousand pounds, and in 1739 to eighty thousand pounds... tho' I now think there are limits beyond which the quantity may be hurtful.
stops.quote_source: Benjamin Franklin, The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Project Gutenberg e-text #148
suggested_refs: The 1748 partnership agreement transferring the operation of Franklin's press

stops.name: Pennsylvania Hospital, the matching fund
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1751; month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Thomas Bond wants a hospital for the sick poor of the province and cannot raise the money, so Franklin carries the subscription to the Assembly with a condition fastened to it: the province will grant two thousand pounds only if private subscribers first raise two thousand of their own. Neither side can hold back its money without losing the other's. Both halves come in and the hospital is built. He writes afterward that he excused himself for this piece of cunning more easily than for any other manoeuvre of his life.
suggested_refs: The 1751 Pennsylvania Assembly act incorporating Pennsylvania Hospital, with its matching-funds clause

stops.name: Philadelphia, the kite and the key
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The earliest account is Joseph Priestley's History and Present State of Electricity (1767), written fifteen years afterward and secondhand; Franklin left no firsthand narrative. The field is not recorded and this coordinate is a central Philadelphia placeholder. Dalibard had already drawn lightning from a pointed rod at Marly-la-Ville in May 1752.
stops.campa: He proposes the experiment in 1750: a pointed iron rod raised high enough to draw the electric fire out of a thundercloud and prove that lightning and the laboratory spark are one substance. France reads the proposal first, and Dalibard performs it at Marly in May 1752. Philadelphia has no spire tall enough, so, the story runs, Franklin raises a silk kite with a wire at its head and a key at the end of the string, and sees the loose threads stand apart. No witness writes it down. Priestley tells it fifteen years later, from hearsay.
suggested_refs: Joseph Priestley, The History and Present State of Electricity (London, 1767), the earliest surviving account
Dalibard's Marly-la-Ville trial, May 1752
sources: Joseph Priestley, History and Present State of Electricity (1767)

stops.name: Philadelphia, joint deputy postmaster general
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1753; month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Postmaster of Philadelphia since 1737, he is made joint deputy postmaster general for all the British colonies, and starts riding the roads himself, surveying routes, timing riders, and fixing the first regular schedules between Boston and Charleston. Under him a letter between Philadelphia and New York takes a day instead of a week. The riders and the schedules he sets down are the ones the committees of correspondence will use twenty years later to move sedition at the speed of the mail. London strips him of the office in 1774.
suggested_refs: Franklin's post office account books and route surveys as joint deputy postmaster general, 1753-1774
sources: United States Postal Service historical records

stops.name: Stadt Huys, the Albany Plan of Union
stops.date_confidence: attested. The Albany Congress sat 19 June to 11 July 1754 and voted approval of the Plan of Union on 10 July. An earlier pass of this research dated the plan to June.
stops.campa: Commissioners from seven colonies meet at Albany's city hall to treat with the Iroquois and to consider common defense. Franklin brings a plan: one president general appointed by the crown, one grand council chosen by the assemblies, with power over treaties, western lands, soldiers, and taxes. The congress approves it on the tenth of July. Every colonial assembly then rejects it for taking too much of their own power, and the crown rejects it for giving too much to the colonies. He is twenty-two years early and refused from both ends at once.
suggested_refs: The text of the Albany Plan of Union, 10 July 1754
Franklin's JOIN, or DIE woodcut, Pennsylvania Gazette, May 1754

stops.name: 36 Craven Street, agent for the Assembly
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1757-1762 residency and the second residency of 1764-1775; the month of arrival defaults to July and the day to 01. Coordinate corrected to the Benjamin Franklin House value, about 110 m from the figure this research first produced.
stops.campa: The Assembly sends him to London to argue that the Penn family's proprietary lands should be taxed like everyone else's. He takes lodgings with the widow Margaret Stevenson at 36 Craven Street, off the Strand, stays five years, goes home for two, and comes back for eleven more. In these rooms he builds a glass armonica, drafts a phonetic alphabet, and lets an anatomist keep a school downstairs. For most of eighteen years he is trying to hold an empire together, and only at the end does he grasp that nobody on this side is listening.
suggested_refs: Benjamin Franklin House, 36 Craven Street, London, the only surviving Franklin residence

stops.name: University of St Andrews, the doctorate
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1759; day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: The university makes the tallow chandler's son a Doctor of Laws for the electrical work, and he is Doctor Franklin from this day forward, though he never sat in any university as a student and has two years of grammar school behind him. Oxford follows in 1762, and the Royal Society has already given him the Copley Medal. The title reaches Paris long before he does, and it is as Docteur Franklin, not as an envoy of a country nobody recognizes, that the salons take him up.
suggested_refs: University of St Andrews degree records, February 1759
The Royal Society Copley Medal award to Franklin, 1753
sources: University of St Andrews degree records
Isaacson, Benjamin Franklin: An American Life

stops.name: Edinburgh, burgess and David Hume
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1759 for the Scottish tour and the freedom of the city; day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: He tours Scotland and Edinburgh makes him a burgess of the city. He sits with David Hume, Lord Kames, and the men building the Scottish Enlightenment, in a kingdom that has taken the road he took: provincial, short of coin, rich in clubs and printing, improving itself by association. The thing he assembled in a Philadelphia back room out of tradesmen is worked here by professors, advocates, and lords of session, and it is the same thing. He is fifty-three and being read by men who did not think a colony could produce a philosopher.
suggested_refs: The Franklin-Hume correspondence, 1759-1772
Edinburgh burgess rolls, 1759
sources: Isaacson, Benjamin Franklin: An American Life

stops.name: Westminster, before the Commons on the Stamp Act
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1766 for the examination and to March 1766 for the repeal; the sitting date of 13 February is standard in the literature but was not confirmed against the Journals of the House of Commons this session.
stops.campa: He stands hours in the House of Commons answering questions, a good many of them planted by friends, about what the colonies will do if the stamp duty stands. Asked what their temper had been before 1763, he says the best in the world. Asked what it is now, he says very much altered. The examination is printed on both sides of the Atlantic and the act is repealed within weeks. He is arguing the case here that he first argued in the pamphlet of 1729, against the same board of trade that will not let a colony make its own money.
stops.quote: That paper-money carries the gold and silver out of the province, and so ruins the country, as experience has shewn, in every colony where it has been practised in any great degree.--This opinion, of its ruining the country, seems to be merely speculative, or not otherwise founded than upon misinformation in the matter of fact.
stops.quote_source: Benjamin Franklin, 'Remarks and Facts Relative to the American Paper-money' (1767), quoting and then rebutting the Board of Trade report of 1764; Complete Works vol. 3, Project Gutenberg e-text #48138
suggested_refs: The Examination of Doctor Benjamin Franklin before an August Assembly, printed 1766
Journals of the House of Commons, February 1766
sources: Journals of the House of Commons, 1766

stops.name: The Cockpit, Whitehall
stops.date_confidence: attested to 29 January 1774.
stops.campa: He has sent private letters of the Massachusetts governor across to Boston, believing they proved the trouble came from Americans and not from London; the letters were printed, and the empire wants a culprit. In the Cockpit at Whitehall the Solicitor General abuses him for an hour before the Privy Council and a gallery of lords who laugh. Franklin stands still, says nothing at all, and is stripped of the post office days later. Tradition adds that he kept the suit he wore, and put it on once more at Passy, on the day France signed the alliance.
suggested_refs: Contemporary accounts of Wedderburn's Cockpit speech, 29 January 1774, collected in Van Doren

stops.name: Independence Hall, the Second Continental Congress
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1775 for his return and election; 10 May is the opening date of the Second Continental Congress.
stops.campa: He lands at Philadelphia after eleven unbroken years in London and is elected to Congress within days. He is sixty-nine, the oldest man in the room by a wide margin, and the only one who has spent a working lifetime inside the government they are preparing to leave. He says little in debate. He sits on the committee for a postal system and is made Postmaster General of a country with no name, running the same roads he surveyed for the crown. His son William, royal governor of New Jersey, stays with the king.
suggested_refs: Journals of the Continental Congress, May 1775

stops.name: Chateau de Ramezay, the Canada mission
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1776 for the arrival of the commissioners at Montreal; the day is given as the commissioners' arrival and should be treated as approximate.
stops.campa: Congress sends three commissioners north to persuade Canada to join the rebellion. Franklin is seventy, gouty, covered in boils, and crosses lakes and portages in the spring thaw to reach Montreal. The commissioners set up in the Chateau de Ramezay with a printer brought along to make propaganda in French. There is no money, the army before Quebec is beaten and sick, and the Canadians will not take Continental paper at any discount. He turns back ill enough to write farewell letters. Canada stays with the king, and he is in Philadelphia again by the end of May.
suggested_refs: The commissioners' reports to Congress from Montreal, spring 1776
Chateau de Ramezay, Montreal

stops.name: The Graff house, marking Jefferson's draft
stops.date_confidence: attested: the committee of five is named 11 June 1776 and the draft is written over the following weeks. Pin inherited byte-identical from thomas_jefferson.journey.json.
stops.campa: The committee of five puts the drafting on Thomas Jefferson, who writes it in a rented parlor at Seventh and Market. Franklin and John Adams go over the sheets and mark them lightly. On the fourth of July, while Congress cuts away a quarter of the text, Franklin sits beside the younger man and tells him about a hatter's signboard whittled down by every friend consulted until nothing was left but a hat. He is seventy, has been edited by committees for forty years, and knows exactly what is being done to Jefferson.
suggested_refs: The reconstructed Graff House at Seventh and Market, Philadelphia

stops.name: Independence Hall, the parchment signed
stops.date_confidence: attested. Congress adopted the Declaration on 4 July 1776; the engrossed parchment was signed by most delegates, Franklin among them, on 2 August. An earlier pass of this research dated his signature to 4 July.
stops.campa: Congress adopts the Declaration on the fourth of July and the engrossed parchment is not signed until the second of August, when Franklin signs among the rest. The line about hanging together or hanging separately is fastened to him by later tellers and by nobody who was in the room. Of all the men who put their names to this sheet, he alone will also sign the treaty of alliance with France, the peace with Britain, and the Constitution: four founding documents, one hand, and no other signer on more than two of them.
suggested_refs: The engrossed Declaration of Independence, National Archives, and the signing of 2 August 1776
sources: National Archives, Declaration of Independence transcript

stops.name: Auray, the landing in Brittany
stops.date_confidence: attested to 3 December 1776 for the landing near Auray after a six-week crossing on the sloop Reprisal.
stops.campa: Congress sends him to France with the Model Treaty in his baggage. The sloop Reprisal takes six weeks, he is seventy and ill for most of it, and he takes sea temperatures for the Gulf Stream out of habit. Weather puts him ashore in a fishing boat near Auray in Brittany rather than at a port. He is landing in a country that has been arming the rebellion in secret since May 1776, through Beaumarchais and a front company, seven months before his arrival. He has not come to open that pipeline. He has come to make it public and legal.
suggested_refs: Franklin's journal of the Reprisal crossing, in the Franklin Papers
The Roderigue Hortalez et Cie arrangement authorised by Vergennes, May 1776
sources: Franklin Papers, journal of the crossing

stops.name: Hotel de Valentinois, Passy
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1777-1785 residency at Passy; month and day of settling in default to February and 01. Pin inherited byte-identical from mesmer.journey.json, which places the 1784 commission's tree trial in this garden.
stops.campa: A financier lends him a wing of a house at Passy, between Paris and Versailles, rent free, and he stays eight years. He wears no wig and a marten fur cap, and Paris decides he is a natural philosopher walked out of the American forests, and puts his face on snuffboxes, rings, medallions, and chamber pots. He sets a private press up in the house and prints passports, bonds, and jokes on it. Behind the fur cap he is running an intelligence war in which one of his own secretaries reports everything to London.
stops.quote: There appeared to me more respect and veneration attached to the character of Dr. Franklin in France, than to that of any other person in the same country, foreign or native.
stops.quote_source: Thomas Jefferson, letter to Dr. William Smith of Philadelphia, written as Franklin's successor as minister to France; Complete Works vol. 3, Project Gutenberg e-text #48138
suggested_refs: The Passy press imprints, 1777-1785
Houdon's bust of Franklin, begun about 1778
sources: Franklin correspondence from Passy, 1777-1785, Franklin Papers

stops.name: Hotel de Coislin, the two treaties signed
stops.date_confidence: attested to 6 February 1778. The place is corrected: an earlier pass of this research put the signing at Franklin's own house in Passy. The treaties were signed at the Hotel de Coislin, called the Hotel de Crillon in English sources, at 4 Place de la Concorde, where a plaque records it.
stops.campa: Saratoga has shown France that the rebels can win, and Vergennes moves. In a house on what is now the Place de la Concorde, Franklin, Silas Deane, and Arthur Lee sign two treaties with the French crown: one of amity and commerce, one of alliance, in which neither party will make a separate peace and France asks no American territory for itself. Covert powder becomes an open army and a fleet. The Marques de Lafayette is in the huts at Valley Forge that winter, writing to Versailles that money alone will not do it.
stops.quote: The count de Vergennes, particularly, gave me repeated and unequivocal demonstrations of his entire confidence in him.
stops.quote_source: Thomas Jefferson, letter to Dr. William Smith of Philadelphia; Complete Works vol. 3, Project Gutenberg e-text #48138
suggested_refs: The Treaty of Alliance and Treaty of Amity and Commerce, 6 February 1778, U.S. National Archives
The commemorative plaque at 4 Place de la Concorde, Paris
sources: U.S. National Archives, Treaty of Alliance with France

stops.name: Palace of Versailles, received by Louis XVI
stops.date_confidence: attested to 20 March 1778. Pin inherited byte-identical from louis_xvi.journey.json and marques_de_lafayette.journey.json.
stops.campa: The king receives the American commissioners, which is recognition made visible: a Bourbon monarch standing surety for a republic founded on the proposition that his kind is unnecessary. Franklin comes in plain brown, without sword and without wig, and a court with a rule for every button makes an exception for him. Louis XVI is twenty-three. Fifteen years from this room the crown will be broken by debts partly contracted here, and the head that grants the audience will come off in a Paris square.
suggested_refs: French court records of the presentation of the American commissioners, 20 March 1778
sources: French court records; Franklin correspondence, March 1778

stops.name: Loge des Neuf Soeurs, Voltaire initiated
stops.date_confidence: attested to 4 April 1778 for Voltaire's initiation and to 1778 for Franklin's own acceptance into the lodge; he is elected Master in 1779 and re-elected in 1780. The lodge's meeting hall varied over its history, so the coordinate is the canonical central Paris pin used across this corpus.
stops.campa: The Paris lodge of the Nine Sisters gathers the astronomers, chemists, and philosophes of the city, and Franklin joins it in the year of the alliance, alongside John Paul Jones and Jean Sylvain Bailly. On the fourth of April he and Antoine Court de Gebelin conduct the initiation of Voltaire, eighty-three years old and a month from death. The lodge elects Franklin Venerable Master in 1779 and again in 1780. The craft whose constitutions he printed in Philadelphia in 1734 is now a room in which he raises money for a war.
suggested_refs: Records of the Loge des Neuf Soeurs, Paris, 1778-1781
sources: Amos, Benjamin Franklin and His French Contemporaries

stops.name: Hotel d'York, the Treaty of Paris
stops.date_confidence: attested to 3 September 1783 at the Hotel d'York, rue Jacob.
stops.campa: Franklin, John Adams, and John Jay sign the peace with Britain in a house on the rue Jacob: independence acknowledged, the boundary run west to the Mississippi, the fisheries kept. They had negotiated separately with London against their instructions from Congress to do nothing without France, and Franklin is the one who then goes to Vergennes, talks the injury down, and asks for a further loan in the same conversation. He is seventy-seven and has been out of the country for the whole of the war.
suggested_refs: The Treaty of Paris, 3 September 1783, U.S. National Archives
Benjamin West's unfinished painting of the American commissioners
sources: U.S. National Archives, Treaty of Paris, 1783

stops.name: Jardin des Tuileries, the hydrogen balloon
stops.date_confidence: attested: Charles and the Robert brothers launched the crewed hydrogen balloon from the Tuileries at 13:45 on 1 December 1783, with Franklin present in the enclosure. The remark about a newborn baby is a reconstruction with no contemporary source and is attached elsewhere to the unmanned Champ de Mars flight of 27 August 1783.
stops.campa: Charles and the Robert brothers rise out of the Tuileries garden under hydrogen with several hundred thousand people watching, and Franklin watches from the enclosure, gouty, in a carriage. He has followed the balloons all year and written about them to correspondents in England, arguing that no army can guard a frontier against five thousand men descending out of the sky. The famous reply about the use of a newborn baby has no contemporary source and is attached by other tellers to a different flight four months earlier.
suggested_refs: Paris press accounts of the Charles and Robert ascent, 1 December 1783
Franklin's balloon letters of 1783 in the Franklin Papers
sources: Isaacson, Benjamin Franklin: An American Life

stops.name: Passy, the blindfolded boy in the garden
stops.date_confidence: attested: the commission's own report states that the king named four physicians of the Faculty of Paris on 12 March 1784, with members of the Academy of Sciences joined to them, and that the trials were conducted partly at Franklin's residence at Passy. The report is signed 11 August 1784. Pin inherited byte-identical from mesmer.journey.json.
stops.campa: Louis XVI names a royal commission to test Franz Anton Mesmer's animal magnetism, and puts Franklin on it with Lavoisier, Bailly, and Guillotin. Franklin is seventy-eight and too gouty to be carried into Paris, so the commission comes out to his garden. They magnetize one tree of four and walk a blindfolded boy down the row; he falls into the crisis at the third tree, which is not the one. The report of the eleventh of August finds no fluid anywhere. Medicine dates the blinded trial to this garden.
suggested_refs: Report of Dr. Benjamin Franklin, and Other Commissioners (London: J. Johnson, 1785)
sources: Report of Dr. Benjamin Franklin, and Other Commissioners, 1784

stops.name: The Hotel de Langeac, Jefferson succeeds him
stops.date_confidence: attested year of Jefferson's appointment as minister to France; the Langeac lease runs 1785-1789. Month and day approximate. Pin inherited byte-identical from thomas_jefferson.journey.json.
stops.campa: Congress relieves him at last and Thomas Jefferson takes the ministry, leasing a house at the top of the Champs-Elysees where the city stops. The younger man spends four years being asked in every Paris salon whether he is Franklin's replacement, and answering that no one replaces him. Franklin has been in France nine years and has drawn loans, gifts, ships, an army, and a peace out of a monarchy that could not afford any of it. He is seventy-nine and going home for the first time in a decade.
stops.quote: 'C'est vous, Monsieur, qui remplacez le Docteur Franklin?' Is it you, sir, who replace Dr. Franklin? I generally answered, 'No one can replace him, sir; I am only his successor.'
stops.quote_source: Thomas Jefferson, letter to Dr. William Smith of Philadelphia; Complete Works vol. 3, Project Gutenberg e-text #48138
suggested_refs: The site of the Hotel de Langeac, corner of the Champs-Elysees and the rue de Berri

stops.name: Southampton, the last sight of William
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1785 for the Southampton meeting; day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Waiting for the ship at Southampton, he sees his son. William Franklin was royal governor of New Jersey, refused to break with the king, was jailed by the Americans, and now lives in London on a crown pension. They meet to divide property and they divide it. The father who acknowledged an illegitimate boy about 1730 and raised him in his own house, who took him out under the thundercloud in 1752, and who got him a governorship by his own credit at court, sails the next day and does not see him again.
suggested_refs: Franklin correspondence, July 1785, in the Franklin Papers

stops.name: Franklin Court, the return and the presidency
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1785 for the return and to 18 October 1785 for his election as President of the Supreme Executive Council of Pennsylvania, which he held until 1788. The day of arrival should be treated as approximate.
stops.campa: He lands in September to cannon, bells, and a crowd down to the wharf, and moves into a house behind Market Street that was built while he was in London and finished while he was in France, and in which he has never lived. Within a month Pennsylvania elects him President of its Supreme Executive Council, the office of governor under another name, and re-elects him twice. He is seventy-nine. The country he has come back to is short of coin again, quarreling about paper money again, and about to call a convention.
stops.quote: I see in the public newspapers of different states frequent complaints of hard times, deadness of trade, scarcity of money, &c. &c. It is not my intention to assert or maintain, that these complaints are entirely without foundation.
stops.quote_source: Benjamin Franklin, 'The Internal State of America' (1786), Complete Works vol. 3, Project Gutenberg e-text #48138
suggested_refs: Franklin Court and the Market Street house, Independence National Historical Park
Pennsylvania Executive Council records, 1785-1788

stops.name: Independence Hall, the oldest delegate signs
stops.date_confidence: attested to 17 September 1787 for the signing; the convention sat from May 1787.
stops.campa: He is eighty-one and carried to the sessions in a sedan chair. He speaks rarely and his speeches are read out for him when he does. At the close he asks every member who still objects to doubt a little of his own infallibility and put his name down, and thirty-nine do. George Washington presides in near silence across the room. Of all the men in this chamber, Franklin alone has also signed the Declaration, the alliance with France, and the peace with Britain. He has less than three years left.
suggested_refs: Madison's Notes of Debates in the Federal Convention of 1787, closing session
sources: Madison, Notes of Debates in the Federal Convention of 1787

stops.name: Franklin Court, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested to 17 April 1790.
stops.campa: He dies at home at eighty-four, in the house behind Market Street, after a long illness. Roughly twenty thousand people walk in the funeral procession, in a city of about forty thousand. The printer's boy who ran out of an indenture at seventeen has been a colonial agent, a postmaster general, a minister to France, and the president of a state, and has spent most of that life outside the country he helped make. He asked in his will for no elaborate honors, and is given the largest funeral the continent has yet held.
stops.quote: 'Sloth, like rust, consumes faster than labour wears, while the used key is always bright,' as poor Richard says. 'But dost thou love life, then do not squander time, for that is the stuff life is made of,' as poor Richard says.
stops.quote_source: Benjamin Franklin, 'The Way to Wealth' (preface to Poor Richard Improved, 1758), Complete Works vol. 3, Project Gutenberg e-text #48138
suggested_refs: Pennsylvania Gazette obituary, April 1790
Franklin's will of 1788
sources: Isaacson, Benjamin Franklin: An American Life

stops.name: Christ Church Burial Ground, the flat stone
stops.date_confidence: attested to 21 April 1790. Coordinate reconciled: two lenses of this research gave 39.9526, -75.1489 and 39.9528, -75.1499, the second of which falls outside the burial ground; the Wikipedia value of 39.95194, -75.14861 is used.
stops.campa: He is laid beside Deborah under a flat marble slab cut, by his own instruction, with nothing but two names and a year. The epitaph he wrote as a young printer, in which his body is the worn cover of a book whose contents will appear again in a corrected edition, is not on the stone; it stays in his papers. In 1858 bronze rails are set into the brick wall so the street can see the grave without entering. Passers-by throw pennies through them onto the slab. Nobody recorded when that began, or why.
stops.quote: THE BODY OF BENJAMIN FRANKLIN, PRINTER. (LIKE THE COVER OF AN OLD BOOK, ITS CONTENTS TORN OUT, AND STRIPT OF ITS LETTERING AND GILDING) LIES HERE FOOD FOR WORMS; YET THE WORK ITSELF SHALL NOT BE LOST, FOR IT WILL (AS HE BELIEVED) APPEAR ONCE MORE IN A NEW AND MORE BEAUTIFUL EDITION CORRECTED AND AMENDED BY THE AUTHOR.
stops.quote_source: Benjamin Franklin's self-composed epitaph, written many years before his death, printed in The Complete Works in Philosophy, Politics and Morals of the late Dr. Benjamin Franklin, vol. 1, Project Gutenberg e-text #48136
suggested_refs: Franklin's grave and the 1858 bronze rails, Christ Church Burial Ground, Fifth and Arch, Philadelphia

stops.name: 36 Craven Street, the bones under the floor
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1998 for the discovery during renovation and to January 2006 for the museum opening; month and day of the find default to 01.
stops.campa: Two centuries after he left it, workmen restoring the Craven Street house find bones from about ten bodies under the basement floor, several of them children. The newspapers reach for the obvious story. The bones belong to William Hewson, the anatomist who married Margaret Stevenson's daughter, ran a school of anatomy in the house while Franklin lodged upstairs, and buried his dissections in a pit because the trade in bodies was illegal. The house opens as a museum in 2006 with the pit left open to view.
suggested_refs: The Craven Street bone pit, Benjamin Franklin House, London
